canonical_statement: The study sought to prospectively validate a prescriptive heparin approach designed to minimize subtherapeutic heparin dosing and achieve adequate anticoagulation within 24 hours, with or without oral anticoagulant therapy.
The study also evaluated the effectiveness and safety of decreasing the heparin dose when APTT prolongation reflected both heparin and warfarin effects.
The study enrolled 199 consecutive patients with proximal deep vein thrombosis documented by venography at Chedoke-McMaster Hospitals, Hamilton, Ontario.

canonical_statement: Before randomization, patients were stratified by prior venous thrombosis and by low versus high bleeding risk; a computer-derived randomized schedule assigned 5 versus 10 days of intravenous heparin therapy.

High bleeding risk was defined by one or more of recent surgery, prior peptic ulcer or gastrointestinal/genitourinary bleeding or bleeding predisposition, thrombotic stroke within 14 days, platelet count below 150×10^9/L, or other reasons such as hepatic failure.

The trial used double blinding: laboratory APTT and prothrombin-time results were reported only to a clinical pharmacist who issued protocol-based dosing recommendations and did not assess patient outcomes.
All patients received a 5000-U intravenous heparin bolus followed by continuous intravenous heparin infusion.

exposures.details: bolus followed by continuous infusion

canonical_statement: Low-bleeding-risk patients began continuous heparin at approximately 40,320 U/24 h (1680 U/h), whereas high-bleeding-risk patients began at approximately 29,760 U/24 h (1240 U/h).

exposures.details: low risk: 1680 U/h = 40,320 U/24 h; high risk: 1240 U/h = 29,760 U/24 h

canonical_statement: Warfarin was continued for 12 weeks and adjusted to an INR of 2.0-3.0; an INR of at least 2.0 was required before heparin discontinuation.
For APTT ≤45 s, the nomogram increased the heparin infusion by 6 mL/h (5760 U/24 h) and repeated APTT in 4-6 hours.
For APTT 46-54 s, the nomogram increased the heparin infusion by 3 mL/h (2880 U/24 h) and repeated APTT in 4-6 hours.
For APTT 55-85 s, the nomogram made no heparin dose change; during the first 24 hours APTT was repeated in 4-6 hours, then at least daily unless subtherapeutic.
For APTT 86-110 s, heparin was stopped for 1 hour, the infusion rate was decreased by 3 mL/h (2880 U/24 h), and APTT was repeated 4-6 hours after restarting.
For APTT >110 s, heparin was stopped for 1 hour, the infusion was decreased by 5760 U/24 h, and APTT was repeated 4-6 hours after restarting.

APTT was measured 4-6 hours after starting heparin and after dose adjustments, as directed during the first 24 hours, and then at least daily; subtherapeutic values triggered repeat testing 4-6 hours after dose increase.

If heparin was interrupted for more than 1 hour, restarting included a 5000-U intravenous bolus, resumption of the prior infusion rate, and repeat APTT 4-6 hours later; shorter interruptions were restarted without a bolus.
All patients were examined daily for the first 10 days and followed for 3 months, including assessments at 3, 6, and 12 weeks; no enrolled patient was unavailable for follow-up.

Suspected recurrent deep vein thrombosis was evaluated with objective vascular testing, and suspected pulmonary embolism was confirmed by high-probability lung scanning or pulmonary angiography when needed.

canonical_statement: Bleeding events were classified as major or minor according to prespecified criteria described in prior publications.

canonical_statement: A persistent subtherapeutic event was an APTT <55 s on or before day 4 that was not followed within 24 hours by an APTT ≥55 s.

outcome.definition: APTT <55 s on or before day 4 not followed within 24 h by APTT ≥55 s

canonical_statement: A persistent supratherapeutic event was an APTT >85 s on or before day 4 that was not followed within 24 hours by an APTT ≤85 s.

outcome.definition: APTT >85 s on or before day 4 not followed within 24 h by APTT ≤85 s

canonical_statement: Repeated-measures analysis of variance was used for APTT and heparin-dose comparisons; Fisher exact testing compared recurrent VTE, bleeding, and supratherapeutic-event frequencies; periodicity was tested with regression methods allowing serial correlation.

Mean APTTs on days 1-5 were 80.7±16.2, 82.6±14.9, 87.0±15.8, 85.2±15.3, and 75.7±16.3 s with simultaneous heparin-warfarin versus 76.1±17.4, 72.0±12.7, 70.7±12.7, 71.4±13.0, and 77.8±13.8 s with heparin alone; the repeated-measures group difference was significant (P<.0001).
Across all patients, mean APTT values remained within the study-prescribed therapeutic range throughout the first 120 hours.
Persistent subtherapeutic APTT for at least 24 hours occurred in 2 of 99 patients (about 2%) receiving simultaneous heparin and warfarin.

canonical_statement: Among patients with persistent supratherapeutic APTT, the mean number of tests and time to return to the therapeutic range were 1.9±1.1 tests and 25.1±20.7 h in the heparin-warfarin group versus 1.6±1.2 tests and 19.5±21.2 h in the heparin-alone group.

Mean heparin doses on days 1-5 were 34,759±7,000, 27,463±8,000, 25,496±8,100, 23,136±7,700, and 21,845±7,400 U/day with simultaneous warfarin versus 36,071±7,200, 30,882±9,100, 31,179±9,100, 31,229±9,400, and 30,800±9,400 U/day with heparin alone; doses differed significantly between groups (P<.0001).
APTT showed a significant diurnal pattern, with a mean peak-to-trough variation of 9.5 s (95% CI 5.9-13.2; P<.0001), peaking at about 3:23 AM and reaching a trough about 12 hours later.

canonical_statement: The authors concluded that the prescriptive heparin protocol minimized prolonged subtherapeutic anticoagulation and delivered effective heparin therapy in both randomized groups.

The authors concluded that supratherapeutic APTT responses were not associated with increased bleeding in this study, contrasting this with prior evidence linking prolonged subtherapeutic APTT responses to recurrent venous thromboembolism.

The authors cautioned that their dose-titration nomogram reflected the specific APTT reagent used in their laboratories and that a clinically useful APTT therapeutic range should correspond to a heparin level of 0.2-0.4 U/mL by protamine titration.
The authors noted that avoiding supratherapeutic APTT values on days 3-5 would have required more than one APTT measurement per day in many patients.
The authors warned that the observed diurnal APTT pattern could lead to inappropriate heparin dose reduction if clinicians overcorrect an early-morning APTT value.
